params.why: the non-prime base must be exactly the s-th power of the prime p
keep the final whole number small enough to work without a calculator

stem: Simplify without using a calculator: $\dfrac{{=B}^{n}\times{=p}^{{=c}}}{{=p}^{{=s}n}}$. Give your answer as a single whole number.
solution: The bases ${=B}$ and ${=p}$ are different, so reduce ${=B}$ to a power of the prime ${=p}$: ${=B}={=p}^{{=s}}$.
Rewrite the power of ${=B}$ with the prime base: ${=B}^{n}=\left({=p}^{{=s}}\right)^{n}={=p}^{{=s}n}$.
Now every term has the same base ${=p}$: $\dfrac{{=p}^{{=s}n}\times{=p}^{{=c}}}{{=p}^{{=s}n}}$.
Multiply in the numerator by adding the exponents: $\dfrac{{=p}^{{=s}n+{=c}}}{{=p}^{{=s}n}}$.
notes: Basic entry point of 'reduce to prime bases', modelled on worked example we02 (p.46): one base is a power of a prime, it is rewritten as (p^s)^n = p^(sn), and the variable exponent then cancels so the answer is a whole number independent of n (we02's own answer is the plain number 2). One skeleton: numerator B^n * p^c over p^(sn), where B = p^s is 4/8/16 (prime 2), 9/27 (prime 3) or 25/125 (prime 5). c runs from 2 up to a cap chosen so the answer p^c never exceeds 128 (c <= 7 for 2, <= 4 for 3, <= 3 for 5), which gives 28 distinct instances; c = 1 is excluded so no exponent of 1 is printed. When c equals s the answer happens to equal B, which is valid. Verified by checking that B^N * p^c / p^(sN) equals p^c for N = 1, 2, 3, 5 on every instance. The stem states 'single whole number' so a blind solver does not answer with a power. No distractors, since the answer is numeric; the catalogued misconception mc:g10m2s2-1-2:merges-factor-into-base concerns merging a plain factor into a base and has no honest place in this skeleton, so it is left for the standard-tier questions where bases are factorised (6^x, 22^x).
